chapter_theme: Aravanar finishes Aputhiran's story, his rebirth from the cow's womb in Savakam and his rise to kingship, and charges Manimekalai not to lay aside the hunger-ending bowl; she enters Puhar's street in a nun's garb, and on her word that a chaste wife's alms are worthiest, the cursed and hungry Kayasandigai sends her to Athirai's house.

cast.role: the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, who tells Aputhiran's story
Madhavi's daughter, now a Buddhist renunciant carrying the bowl
Manimekalai's mother, now a Buddhist renunciant
Manimekalai's companion, one of her two 'mothers'
the earlier owner of the bowl, reborn from a cow's womb as king of Savakam
the golden-horned cow that once sheltered Aputhiran and bears him again in Savakam
the sage of Savakam who foretells Aputhiran's birth and gives the child to the king
the childless king of Savakam who raises Aputhiran as his son
the ascetics living at the Chakravala kottam
the image painted by a god on the pillar, which speaks oracles
the crowd of Puhar's little folk, rakes and libertines
a vidyadhara woman cursed with an insatiable hunger

manimekalai:15:1-14.reading: Aravanar goes on with Aputhiran's story: the good cow that once sheltered him, golden-horned and golden-hoofed, came to the great sage Manmukhan by the white mountain of Savakam and, before it had ever calved, gave its milk to every creature, and the sage who knew the three times foretold that from its womb would come a protector of lives to make the rain abound, born not with the cord about him but within a golden egg.
manimekalai:15:1-14.nuance: The cow nurses all creatures before calving (ஈனாமுன்னம்), so its gift of milk precedes and announces the birth; and the prophecy names the newborn's work as bringing rain and guarding lives (11-12), the very want that drove Aputhiran from Madurai toward rainless Savakam in the previous kaathai.
manimekalai:15:1-14.event: In Savakam a golden-horned cow gives its milk to all creatures before calving, and the sage Manmukhan foretells that a protector of lives will be born from its womb in a golden egg.

manimekalai:15:15-28.reading: Aravanar says that the one who gave up his life on Manipallavam, because his steady heart never let go of the cow that had once guarded and fed him, was born from that cow's womb to the gods' delight, one alone for this jambu island, and he tells the season of the birth, a day of spring fixed to the Bodhi lord's own, when a rain of holy water and flowers fell over the whole earth without a cloud.
manimekalai:15:15-28.nuance: The cause given for the womb he is born from is a bond of the mind: he 'did not let go' of the cow with an unwavering heart (17-18), which reads as gratitude carried through death; kaathai 14 had given his dying intent to sustain lives as the cause of the birth itself. The date at 23-26 is reckoned by the season, the sun in Taurus and the Buddha's day; line 25 (மீனத்து இடைநிலை மீனத்து அகவையின்) is obscure, and the reading does not rest on it.
manimekalai:15:15-28.event: Aputhiran, who died on Manipallavam, is born from the cow's womb in Savakam in spring, and holy water and flowers rain over the earth without clouds.

claims.claim: one who dies with a being held unwavering in mind is reborn from that being's womb

manimekalai:15:15-28.unit_note: End moved from line 30 to 28: line 28 (சொரிந்தது) closes the account of the rain, and the quotation at 29-30 belongs with its speakers, the ascetics named at 31-32.

manimekalai:15:29-45.reading: The ascetics of the Chakravala kottam, marvelling that such wonders were seen though it was not the time of a Buddha's coming, went through the thick dark to ask the image a god had painted on the pillar, which told them that the one who died on Manipallavam had arisen in Savakam to save lives and that Aravanan knew his story; that, Aravanar says, is what set his tongue to telling it; and the king of Savakam, bowing at Manmukhan's feet and saying that he had no child and had gained a son by the sage's grace, raised the boy, who became king since the wealth of rule was his.
manimekalai:15:29-45.nuance: Aravanar names the pillar image as the source that sends the knowledge to him (36-39), so his account of a rebirth across the sea is given a witness; the childless king takes the egg-born child as a gift of a sage's grace (42-43), and the poem passes over how a foundling took the throne with the bare remark that the wealth of kingship was his (44).
manimekalai:15:29-45.event: The pillar image tells the ascetics of the Chakravala kottam that Aputhiran is reborn in Savakam, and the childless king of Savakam takes him from the sage Manmukhan as a son, and he becomes king.

claims.claim: wonders such as a cloudless rain of flowers belong to the time when a Buddha appears on earth

manimekalai:15:29-45.unit_note: Start moved from line 31 to 29 so that the ascetics' quoted marvel (29-30, ending என) sits with their naming at 31-32; end moved from line 46 to 45, where ஆயினன் அவன் தான் closes the account of his kingship, since line 46 opens a rhetorical pair completed at 47.

manimekalai:15:46-54.reading: Aravanar asks whether the king of heaven lacks his share or the king of the just sceptre lacks grace, observes that though the Kaveri swells and spreads its water a season of want has come on every living thing, and tells Manimekalai that to put away the bowl that ends the world's great hunger, as the gods put away the leftover nectar the white waves gave them, is not fitting.
manimekalai:15:46-54.nuance: The two questions (46-47) seem to clear both the god of rain and the just king, so the want of 48-50 is given no culprit; the sense of துய்ப்பிலன் is uncertain. The comparison at 51-52 turns the gods' nectar, saved and kept after they had eaten, into the type of a hoard withheld from the hungry.
manimekalai:15:46-54.event: Aravanar tells Manimekalai that want has come despite the flowing Kaveri and that she must not lay the bowl aside.

claims.claim: it is wrong to keep back a means of ending the world's hunger, as the gods kept back the leftover nectar

manimekalai:15:46-54.unit_note: Units 31-46 and 47-60 were recut: this unit starts at 46, where the rhetorical pair begins, and ends at 54, where தகாது' என closes Aravanar's speech.

manimekalai:15:55-70.reading: When the sage has spoken, Manimekalai bows with her mothers, takes up the divine bowl and goes in a bhikkhuni's garb into the great street, and the town's little folk, rakes and libertines crowd round with noise, pitying her as men once pitied Yugi the Brahmin of Ujjain in a sickness unsuited to his form, when he freed the Vatsa king of Kosambi from his bonds, and they grieve that the honey-haired girl Udayakumaran had set his heart on has come carrying a begging bowl.
manimekalai:15:55-70.nuance: The crowd sees disgrace in the bowl (சிந்தை நோய் கூர), while the simile likens her garb to Yugi's feigned disease, a guise that hid a plan to free a king from prison; the onlookers are the same 'rakes and libertines' (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும்) who in kaathai 14 idled in Aputhiran's hall once plenty made his bowl useless. Udayakumaran is only named, not present.
manimekalai:15:55-70.event: Manimekalai bows with her mothers and goes into the great street in a nun's garb with the bowl, and the townsfolk crowd round, grieving that the girl the prince loved now carries a begging bowl.
manimekalai:15:55-70.unit_note: Start moved from line 61 to 55, where மாதவன் உரைத்தலும் opens the narration after Aravanar's speech; end moved from 74 to 70, where சிந்தை நோய் கூர closes the crowd's sentence begun at 59, before Manimekalai speaks at 71.

manimekalai:15:71-86.reading: The flowering branch Madhavi bore says with full gladness that to receive the alms good chaste wives give is a thing of great worth, and Kayasandigai, a woman of the northern vidyadhara city who, her harsh deed ripening through a sage's curse by a stream on southern Pothiyil, wanders in unending fierce hunger, tells her that Athirai stands alone among the house-dwelling wives whose chastity gives rain, like one lotus risen above the rest in a pool, and that this is her house, which she should enter.
manimekalai:15:71-86.nuance: The nun's first choice is of a giver, not of food: the bowl is to take its first alms from a pathini, and the one who points the way is herself a woman suffering the fruit of her own deed. Manimekalai is named here as Madhavi's child (மாதவி ஈன்ற) just as she seeks a chaste wife's alms, and Kayasandigai's praise of Athirai's rain-giving karpu (77) answers her claim at once.
manimekalai:15:71-86.event: Manimekalai says that alms from a chaste wife are worthiest, and Kayasandigai, a vidyadhara woman cursed to endless hunger, tells her to enter Athirai's house.

claims.claim: alms received from a chaste wife are of the greatest worth
a wife's chastity brings the rain
a grave deed ripens through a sage's curse into suffering

manimekalai:15:71-86.unit_note: Start moved from line 75 to 71, so that Manimekalai's claim (71-74, ending எனக்) stands with the reply it prompts; the unit runs to the kaathai's end.

links.note: In kaathai 14 Aputhiran hears that rain has failed in Savakam and sets out to carry his bowl there; here the cow's sage foretells, in Savakam itself, a protector born to make the rain abound and guard lives (மழை வளம் சுரப்பவும் மன் உயிர் ஓம்பவும்).
links.teaches: The errand the shipwreck cut short is fulfilled by rebirth: Aputhiran reaches the rainless land not as a beggar with a bowl but as its rain-bringing king, so the epic moves his charity from alms to kingship across a death.

links.note: Kaathai 14 says he left his body on Manipallavam with the intent to sustain unappeased lives and arose from a cow's womb in Savakam; here the cause of that womb is that his unwavering heart never let go of the cow that had guarded him (ஒல்கா உள்ளத்து ஒழியான் ஆதலின்).
links.teaches: Read together, the two passages give rebirth two causes at two levels: compassion for all lives decides the land and the work, while a personal debt of gratitude decides the very mother, so a private bond shapes the birth inside a universal vow.

links.note: In kaathai 14 Indra's gift of plenty left Aputhiran's bowl with no takers and his hall silent; here Aravanar says want has come again despite the Kaveri and forbids laying the same bowl aside.
links.teaches: The bowl's worth is shown to depend wholly on there being hunger: plenty once made it useless and drove its keeper to death, and now a season of want is the reason it must come back into a girl's hands.

links.note: The couplet calls relieving the destitute's ruinous hunger the place where a man of wealth should store it; Aravanar likens laying aside the hunger-ending bowl to the gods keeping back their leftover nectar, and calls it unfit.
links.teaches: The couplet keeps a giver's profit in view by making charity a kind of saving, while the epic's bowl has no owner to profit and treats any keeping back as the gods' hoard, so feeding the hungry is pressed past prudence into a duty with no return.

gains.a: Aravanar's rule against laying the bowl aside gains a contrast with the ethics book's view of charity as a store for the giver, which shows how far the bowl's keeper is from any owner's interest.
gains.b: The couplet's banking image gains a case with no depositor at all, a bowl whose holder gains nothing, which exposes the self-regard the image keeps.

links.note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; Aravanar asks whether the king of heaven or the just-sceptred king has failed, and says want has come though the Kaveri flows. The link holds on the reading that the questions at 46-47 clear both.
links.teaches: The epic grants the Kural's premise that a just king brings plenty and still finds hunger in his land, so hunger becomes a want no sceptre cures and the place where the renouncer's bowl, not the king, must act.

gains.a: The rhetorical questions at 46-47 are explained: they answer the Kural's doctrine that want betrays a bent sceptre, which is why the speaker must clear the king before calling for the bowl.
gains.b: The couplet's promise of plenty under a just king gains a counter-case where both god and king are blameless and the people still hunger.

links.note: When Aputhiran's hall fell silent in plenty, rakes, libertines and idlers (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும் விட்டேற்றாளரும்) took it over with dice; here the same rakes and libertines (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும்) crowd round Manimekalai as she enters the street with the bowl.
links.teaches: The town's idlers mark both ends of the bowl's story: they fill the hall when the bowl is useless and gather in pity when it returns, so the bowl's renewed use is first met by the very crowd that had displaced it.

links.note: The Udayana Kumara Kaviyam tells how Yugi, feigning madness and sense by turns, passed along the great streets with crowds about him to the prison where the Vatsa king was held; the Manimekalai likens the crowd's pity for Manimekalai with her bowl in the great street to the pity felt for Yugi's feigned sickness when he freed the Vatsa king.
links.teaches: The simile reads the nun's garb as a disguise like Yugi's, pitied by onlookers yet hiding a purpose of release, and the later Jain epic's street scene shows the crowd and the prison that the Manimekalai's one-line allusion assumes its hearers know.

links.note: The couplet says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow; Manimekalai enters the street with a begging bowl and, at 71-74, calls receiving a chaste wife's alms a thing of great worth, while the crowd grieves at the sight.
links.teaches: The town's grief voices the Kural's shame of asking, and the nun's claim answers it with a begging that asks nothing for herself and seeks the worthiest giver, so the two disagree about whether all asking shames the asker.

gains.a: The crowd's pity (சிந்தை நோய் கூர) is shown to rest on the ethics books' contempt for begging, which the nun's alms round has to overcome.
gains.b: The couplet's limit case, begging even for a cow, meets a beggar whose bowl came down from a cow-born king and feeds others, a case its absolute rule does not consider.

links.note: Kayasandigai sends Manimekalai to Athirai's house as the one wife of rain-giving chastity; the next kaathai ends with Athirai putting the first food, the 'medicine for life', into the bowl (ஆதிரை இட்டனள் ஆருயிர்மருந்து).
links.teaches: Manimekalai's rule that the bowl's first alms must come from a pathini is carried out at once, and the giver chosen is a wife whose husband had left her for a courtesan, so the courtesan's daughter's bowl is first filled by such a wife.

links.note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; Kayasandigai praises Athirai as standing alone among the house-dwelling wives of rain-giving chastity (வான் தருகற்பின் மனை உறை மகளிரின்) and so the right giver of the bowl's first alms.
links.teaches: The epic takes the couplet's rain-giving wife as a known type and makes it a rank, one supreme among many, and a qualification for feeding a Buddhist bowl, so domestic chastity is set to work for the renouncer's charity.

gains.a: Kayasandigai's phrase is shown to rest on the Kural's claim, so her choice of Athirai appeals to a test the hearers already accept.
gains.b: The couplet, which speaks of any such wife, gains a use: chastity's power over the rain becomes a standard for whose alms are worthiest, a ranking the couplet does not make.

links.note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki lists the chaste wives of Puhar and their wonders as she turns on Madurai; here Kayasandigai names Athirai as the one who stands alone among Puhar's rain-giving wives.
links.teaches: The pathinis of the same city serve the twin epics in opposite ways: Kannaki calls on them to back a curse that burns a city, while Manimekalai seeks one of them to give the first food to a bowl that feeds it.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose virtue carries power
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர், line 73)

source_issues: Lines 51 and 81: the build removed a leftover HTML quote mark at the start of the line; the Tamil otherwise reads cleanly.
The break score of 3 after line 46 falls inside a rhetorical pair (46-47, துய்ப்பிலன்கொல்லோ? / அருளிலன்கொல்லோ); the units were recut at 45 and 54.
The kaathai ends at line 86 with காரிகை தான் என், the closing particle, after the speaker's name has been held back from என்றனள் at line 80.
Line 25 (மீனத்து இடைநிலை மீனத்து அகவையின்) is obscure in this text, and the date it gives cannot be fixed from it.
